fact_label: Burning season disrupts daily routine Jan-Apr
unit: µg/m³ (PM2.5, annual northern-Thailand baseline to March 2026 peak)
notes: PM2.5 peaked at 188 µg/m³ in Chiang Mai in March 2026 (~35-37x the WHO annual guideline of 5 µg/m³), ranking it the world's most polluted city on multiple occasions that month (iqair.com, 2026-03-04; openthemagazine.com, 2026). Not a one-bad-year event: northern Thailand's PM2.5 annual average sits at 33 µg/m³ (2019 data), with a seasonal average of 70 µg/m³ during burning-season months specifically, and acute March spikes stacking on top of that baseline (thailandhilltribeholidays.com, 2026) — the value_num range here spans that annual baseline (33) to the recorded peak (188). Real pace-of-life effect, not just an air-quality statistic: overview.md's own extracted narrative describes a March morning routine of checking an air-quality app before deciding whether to open a window or go outside at all — the season runs roughly Jan-Apr, about a third of the year, arriving in the same weeks the file's own climate section calls the mildest by temperature. Trajectory marked worsening/recurring per red-flags.md's own explicit framing ('recurring annually, no sign of structural improvement found this pass') — trend note, not a claim of a specific year-over-year severity increase. Contrast: Bangkok's dry-season PM2.5 runs materially lower, 28-33 µg/m³ in early 2026 (see TH-bangkok rows) — this is a genuinely Chiang Mai-specific severity, not a shared northern-Thailand baseline.

notes: Correction 2026-08-24 ([specialist], citation-integrity fix): the 118.5:1 tourist-to-inhabitant ratio was previously misattributed to theborderlessoffice.com/aseannow.com. Re-checked directly: it actually traces to MoneyTransfers.com's own study, 'The Most & Least “Over-Touristed” Destinations Around The World' (Yasmin Purnell, last updated 2026-04-20), which states Phuket is "officially the most overloaded city in the world, with a staggering 118.5 tourists to every 1 inhabitant." Their stated methodology: international-arrivals data from a Euromonitor International study, population data from World Population Review, no published formula or year-of-data breakdown; the study itself flags that 'not many tourists are staying in the city itself for long,' meaning the figure likely includes transit passengers -- a real limitation on what it says about day-to-day overcrowding actually felt by residents. The separate 'traffic unbearable, every journey feels like an ordeal' description remains genuinely corroborated by theborderlessoffice.com's own account (still 403-blocked on direct fetch, read via search-cache summary only) and the aseannow.com expat-forum thread describing six longtime expats leaving Phuket over traffic. Trajectory marked worsening per the traffic accounts' own framing, not independently trend-confirmed against a prior-year baseline. Honest counterbalance: other 2026 sources in the same search pass describe Phuket as 'fantastic for digital nomads if you pick the right area' (see community-network.md in full).

fact_label: Fiber broadband speed, real-world household average
notes: Correction 2026-08-24 ([specialist], citation-integrity fix): the two providers' area-coverage lists were previously swapped. Re-fetched phuketexpatguide.com's actual internet guide (/blog/phuket-internet-speeds/) directly to confirm: AIS Fibre is the most-recommended provider, strongest in Bang Tao, Laguna, Chalong, and northern Phuket Town (~฿500/month for 100 Mbps, ~฿1,200/month for 1 Gbps). True Move H (True Online) has particularly strong infrastructure in Patong, the south of the island, and parts of Phuket Town (~฿480/month for 100 Mbps, ~฿1,100/month for 1 Gbps) -- a shorter, geographically distinct list from AIS's, not the wider one. The page's own broader area-by-area speed/rating table also covers Kamala, Rawai/Nai Harn, Surin/Cherng Talay, and Kata/Karon as good-to-moderate fibre-available areas, but does not attribute those specifically to either named ISP -- a real, not-filled-in gap, not restated here as fact. Starlink is a real fallback where fiber coverage is thin, typically 100-200 Mbps down / 10-20 Mbps up, 25-55ms latency. A direct TestMy.net pull for Phuket's own measured (not advertised-plan) average was attempted and blocked (403) -- genuine gap, not filled with an estimate; this row uses advertised/typical real-world household figures instead, named as such rather than presented as a measured-speed-test result.

fact_label: Measured fixed broadband speed (Ookla)
notes: Ookla Speedtest Global Index: Bangkok fixed broadband 312.75 Mbps download / 254.02 Mbps upload, 5ms latency, ranked #9 globally, as of May 2026 (via speedtest-index aggregator sites) — closed as a gap in prose 2026-07-09 ([specialist]), extracted as its own fact row this pass (mechanical extraction, not new research). Mobile broadband, same source/date: 191.82 Mbps down / 32.87 Mbps up, 17ms latency, ranked #42 globally (not separately value_num-encoded here — see a future row if mobile needs its own criterion cell). Bangkok's fixed-line figure runs meaningfully above the national blended average (272.65 Mbps down, see TH:national rows), consistent with it being the country's most infrastructure-dense metro. Condos/coworking spaces (The Hive Thonglor, JustCo, True Digital Park Punnawithi) routinely offer 500 Mbps-1 Gbps fiber on top of this.
